2027-07-17.title: Saturday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt
His steadfast love endures for ever
He will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick
2027-07-17.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). On Saturdays in Ordinary Time, when there is no obligatory memorial, the optional memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary may be kept. Psalm 136 has the same numbering in the Lectionary and the NRSV. The Malayalam month of Karkidakam, the month of the heaviest monsoon rain, begins about now. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-17.verse: A bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice.
theo: Today's first reading is the departure. After the last night in Egypt the people of Israel march out from Rameses to Succoth, “about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.” They carry unleavened dough, because they were “driven out of Egypt and could not wait.” The Bible records the exact length of the slavery, “four hundred thirty years,” and says that on the very day the years were completed, “all the companies of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.” There is one detail that is easy to miss: “A mixed crowd also went up with them.” Not all who left Egypt were descendants of Jacob; there were other slaves and foreigners who saw that the God of Israel was acting and went along with them. From the start the people of God has been bigger than a single family. And then comes the heart of the passage: “That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. That same night is a vigil to be kept for the Lord by all the Israelites throughout their generations.” The night belonged to the Lord, who kept watch; now the people keep watch in return. For this reason the Jewish people stay up on Passover night to tell the story, and the Church, in the same spirit, keeps the greatest vigil of the year on Holy Saturday night, when the Easter Candle is lit and the deacon sings that this is the night when God led our ancestors out of Egypt and the night when Christ broke the chains of death. The psalm repeats the refrain after every line, “for his steadfast love endures forever,” and names what he did: “brought Israel out from among them … with a strong hand and an outstretched arm,” and “remembered us in our low estate.”

In the Gospel the shadow falls. After the argument about the sabbath, “the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.” Some of the Pharisees, we must remember, were friends of Jesus, and some warned him of danger; Matthew is speaking of the party that plotted against him. What does Jesus do? “When Jesus became aware of this, he departed.” He does not argue, he does not threaten, and he does not run away in fear. He withdraws, and goes on healing: “Many crowds followed him, and he cured all of them.” And he commands silence: “he ordered them not to make him known.” Matthew explains why by quoting the first Servant Song of Isaiah: “Here is my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles.” The King is a Servant, and the Servant is gentle: “He will not wrangle or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until he brings justice to victory.” A bruised reed is a stem that is cracked and about to snap, and a smoldering wick is a flame about to die; they are pictures of the weak, the discouraged and the sinful, and Jesus does not throw them away: he bends over them to heal. And the passage ends with the word that rings like the “mixed crowd” of Exodus: “in his name the Gentiles will hope.” The people who left Egypt were already a mixed company, and the Servant opens the way for all nations. Both readings are about God's quiet, patient strength: the night watch of the Lord over his people, and the gentle hand over the bruised reed.
outline: Ask: who keeps vigil for you at night, and for whom do you keep it?
God watches over his people on the night of the Exodus, and we keep watch with him.
The people of God is wider than one family: the foreigners who went out with Israel, and all nations who hope in his name.
He does not answer a plot with force; he withdraws and heals.
The Servant who does not break the weak and does not put out the faintest flame.
“A bruised reed he will not break.”
live: Before sleeping tonight, spend ten minutes in silence, thanking God for watching over your day and asking him to watch over those who are alone tonight: the sick, the night-shift workers, the travellers.
Think of a person who is discouraged or fragile, a bruised reed, and give them an encouraging word or small kindness today. Do not argue with them; strengthen them.
2027-07-17.prayer: Lord God, you kept a night of vigil to bring your people out of slavery, and your steadfast love endures for ever. Watch over us tonight and always, and teach us to keep watch with you in prayer. Lord Jesus, chosen Servant, beloved of the Father, you did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick: be gentle with our weakness, and make us gentle with the weakness of others. Open your house to the mixed crowd of all nations, and let your name be the hope of every people. Amen.
altar: The Mass is the Church's vigil and the Church's Exodus. We come out of the week to gather around the Lord's table, and what we celebrate is a passage: from slavery to life, from death to resurrection, in Christ. Before Communion we say, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and the Lamb who is gentle with the bruised reed feeds us with himself. Every Mass is a small Easter night.

quick: The Israelites leave Egypt after four hundred and thirty years, with a mixed crowd of other people, and the Lord keeps vigil that night.
Some Pharisees plot to destroy Jesus; he withdraws, heals the crowds and asks them to keep silent.
Matthew quotes Isaiah: the Servant is gentle, he will not break a bruised reed, and the Gentiles will hope in his name.
2027-07-17.action: Say a kind and encouraging word today to someone who is discouraged.
2027-07-17.question: When I meet someone who is fragile, do I snap the reed, or do I bend down to help?

family.explain: Jesus was kind to everybody, especially the people who were sad, sick or weak. The prophet Isaiah had said that God's Servant would be like that: he would never break a bent reed, or put out a flame that was nearly gone. Think of a candle that is nearly out. A gentle hand shields it, and it burns again. Jesus is like that with us. When we are sad or have done wrong, he does not shout; he helps us to burn brightly again.
family.intention: We pray for people who are sad, lonely or discouraged, and we ask Jesus to make us gentle with others.
family.ask: Ask: “Who in our family or school is feeling bent or tired this week? What small thing can we do to help them shine again?”

illus: In a village in Wayanad, a retired schoolteacher kept an old kerosene lamp in her house although there was electricity. When the power failed in the monsoon nights she would light it, and the children of the neighbourhood would gather. The wick was always almost gone, she said, and a breath too strong would put it out, so she lit it with a cupped hand. She told the children that one learns more from the weak flame than from the strong light, because it teaches you to shield what is small. Years later, one of those children became a nurse and said that she remembered the lamp whenever she met a patient who had no strength left. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you who keep watch over us, strengthen us in your gentleness. Lord Jesus, chosen Servant, teach us your way. Amen.
share: That was for the Lord a night of vigil (Exodus 12:42). When have I felt that God was keeping watch over me in a dark time?
A mixed crowd also went up with them (Exodus 12:38). Who is on the edge of my community, and how can I welcome them?
He will not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). Whom do I know who is a bruised reed, and what does Jesus' way suggest that I do?
pm.resp: His steadfast love endures for ever.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a gentle mother to the weak, the doubting and the wounded.
For those who work at night, and those who keep watch beside the sick and dying.
For refugees, migrants and strangers who journey among us, that they may find welcome.
For people who are discouraged, depressed or on the brink of giving up.
For our group, that we may be gentle, patient and hopeful, like Christ the Servant.
pm.close: Father, you watched over your people in the night and sent your Servant to heal. Make us gentle with the fragile and faithful in our watching. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, picture the night the people leave Egypt. After four hundred and thirty years, in a hurry, with unleavened dough on their backs, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. And the Bible says: that was for the Lord a night of vigil (Exodus 12:42). Think of that: while the people are rushing and afraid, God is awake. He is keeping watch. That is the first good news: when you cannot sleep, when you are afraid, someone is awake over you. And so every year the people keep that night, and every year at Easter we keep the greatest vigil of all.

Notice also: a mixed crowd also went up with them (Exodus 12:38). It was not only the family of Jacob. Other slaves, other peoples, saw what God was doing and joined in. God's people has never been a closed club. In Jesus, the prophet says, the Gentiles will hope (Matthew 12:21). The door is wide. Who is the mixed crowd today, the migrant worker, the newcomer in the parish, the one who does not look like us? Let us make room.

In the Gospel there is a plot. The enemies of Jesus meet and decide to destroy him. And what does Jesus do? He leaves. He does not shout, he does not fight. He goes on healing. Matthew says that he fulfils Isaiah: he will not wrangle or cry aloud; he will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick (Matthew 12:19–20). Brothers and sisters, we are all bruised reeds in some way: weak, discouraged, close to snapping. And he does not break us. He does not put out the little flame of our faith, even when it is only smoking. He bends over it and protects it with his hand.

Let us take that gentleness with us. When we meet someone who is weak, let us not snap them; let us shield the flame. And when we ourselves are bruised, let us remember that the Lord who watched over Israel in the night is watching over us, and that his steadfast love endures for ever. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago God's people had to leave Egypt in a great hurry, in the middle of the night. They were scared. But God stayed awake all night, looking after them! Many other people joined them too, because they saw that God was good. Years later, Jesus was kind in a special way. The prophet said that Jesus would never break a bent reed, or put out a little flame. Imagine a candle nearly out: Jesus shields it with his hand and it shines again. When a friend is sad or a bit broken, you can be like Jesus. Be gentle, say something kind, and help the little flame to shine.

intro: Theme: “A bruised reed he will not break.”
A night of vigil for a mixed crowd leaving Egypt, and the gentle Servant who does not put out the smoldering wick.

q: That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. That same night is a vigil to be kept for the Lord by all the Israelites throughout their generations.
Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
points.apply: Make a ten-minute vigil of prayer before bed this week, and entrust to God someone who is alone tonight.

He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

concl: The Lord keeps vigil to bring his people out of Egypt, and a mixed crowd goes out with them: his people is wider than one family.
Jesus answers plotting with healing; the gentle Servant does not break the bruised reed, and in his name the nations hope.
2027-07-17.resolve: Welcome one stranger and encourage one discouraged person this week, and keep a short vigil of prayer one evening.
